newsitem.title: CHINA: China seen pushing to introduce market forces.
newsitem.headline: China seen pushing to introduce market forces.

text.p: China's decision to reform its huge agricultural system by raising the price the state pays for grain to market rates is part of a renewed bid to introduce market forces, officials said on Thursday.

Politburo member Li Tieying announced the ambitious reform in a speech in the southern pilot city for reform, Shenzhen, when he outlined some of Beijing's plans for 1997 to dismantle Stalinist-style central planning in favour of market forces.
"Next year, there will be only one price for grain purchasing," a government spokesman said from Shenzhen.
He declined to give further details of how China would unify the state grain purchasing price with the market price, but voiced apparent unease about the difficult, and potentially risky, process.

"Now it is hard to see the effect of unifying the price," he said. "If the unified price is higher than the original purchasing price, then this will be good for famers' interests, but if it is lower, then it will sap the incentive among farmers to plant," he said.
China's central authorities still buy a certain amount of grain from farmers at set prices below the market rates to ensure ample stores in state granaries.

Since paramount leader Deng Xiaoping launched economic reform in 1978, Beijing's communist leaders have tried -- and failed -- to free grain prices, falling foul of fears that spiralling prices would take much food beyond the pockets of many of China's 1.2 billion people and spark social unrest.
They have raised purchasing prices, narrowing the gap with market rates, but have been unable to eliminate the difference entirely.
With a record harvest of 480 million tonnes forecast for this year and with market prices falling closer to the state level, analysts said the time was ripe to unify the system.

Officials declined to say whether the government would also take the opportunity to force urban consumers to pay the market price for grain, thus relieving state coffers of the burden of huge subsidies when plentiful supplies could curb price rises.
China's leaders have long feared that difficulties in selling grain would dampen farmers' incentive to plant, placing in jeopardy China's ability to feed itself without resorting to huge imports.
Grain was not the only agricultural commodity to see a market reform, said Li, minister in charge of the State Commission for Restructuring the Economy.
Market forces would govern cotton purchasing, he said.
"China has decided to use cotton trade fairs...to replace the state-planned system," said one official who declined to be identified.
In the past, the state controlled all cotton buying and marketing, the official said.
"If the state asked A to buy, then A had to buy, if they asked B to sell, then B had to sell," he said.
"But now sellers and buyers can talk at the trade fair," he said. The first trade fair under this new system was held in early November in the central city of Zhengzhou.

China's official forecast for the 1996 cotton harvest is 3.5 million tonnes, down more than 1.0 million tonnes from 1995 because many farmers have been reluctant to plant because of unattractive state prices.
